title: The Count That Isn't Mine
blurb: Glasshouse take away Wren's warning, and the only way through is to draw on someone else's count.

blocks.text: Somebody is being sick into the kiln ash bucket.
Properly sick. The bucket is tin, and it rings like a cheap plate every time he heaves.
Then the Warden, flat as a floor chart: "Kilnyard. Your registration for the second Half."
Sef doesn't look round. "Halloway and Carrick, Dampers. Tewkes on to Call."

The one in the bucket is Dov Carrick. Loudest Caller in the Cellar Ring. He has just been named a Damper, and in about ninety counts he has to stand half a wave from me and draw a note into his body on a count.
His count. Not mine.
I have never drawn on anybody's count but my own. Tonight I don't get the choice.
It starts with glass.

Glasshouse come down our stair two hours before that bucket, five of them in leather aprons with the burn-holes patched. Their Scribe has forearms shiny with old scald. Sef has them all named before the last one's off the bottom step.
"Scribe's the Gaffer," he says. "Callers: tall one in the scarf is Frost, short one's Cullet. Dampers are brothers. Penhale and Penhale. The Panes."
"Why the Panes?"
"You can see straight through them. Watch."
I watch. While the Warden beats the walls for bloom, the Penhale brothers walk our floor chart with a knotted string, stand to stand, and chalk numbers on their wrists.
"They've copied us," says Dov. He sounds flattered.

"They've copied the shape of us," says Sef. "Three things. One, they've heard about the ghost quells. Two, they think it's a formation: two Dampers in one beam, the right gap, done. Three, they've measured gaps. Nobody's measured a note."
I do my wall test while they measure. Knuckle and palm, all the way round. Dry. Kiln-warm at the back by the old flue, cool by the stair. Same as last week.

Then the Last Stand, because I can't not. It still rocks a finger's breadth. Still rings flat. Nobody has re-bedded it, and I'm not allowed to touch it. Marten stays off it again. No Last Plate tonight, and no Hand-Stills.
"Pace five," says the Warden.
Five. Good. I know every pair on this floor at five.
What I don't know yet is that the Panes are the show. The real plan is Frost.
Frost Raises. Hand up. One count.
No lead-in.

Nothing comes up through my soles during the Raise. No hum. No pitch. The floor is as quiet as a shut door. Then the note is voiced, and the floor-tell arrives, and by then the Raise is over and my feet are nailed where they stand.

A cold throw. It wanders up to two semitones, either way, and Frost won't know which until it's out. Neither will I. That's the whole idea. Somebody at Glasshouse has worked out that I read the lead-in, and they've taken it off me.
It's not a stupid idea. It's a mason's idea. If you can't make the face true, hide it.
This one drifts sharp. I feel it climb, a hair high, then more. It hits our Last Plate a semitone and a half over Oduya's peg and rattles like a dropped spoon.

"That's what it costs her," says Sef behind me, low. "One, cold drifts. Two, it has to land within a semitone of our peg to Peal. Three, she can't aim a drift. Half of what she throws cold goes nowhere."
"And the other half?"
"Other half's yours."
Oduya walks the peg a semitone at the Breath. Then back. Then up again.
"A cold throw is a cook who will not taste the soup," she says, when she catches me looking. "Salt and pray. I am simply moving the pot."
Dov's turn. He gives the Lamplighter a lead-in like an organ in a chapel, big and proud, and the Penhales hop to their chalked stands, both in the beam, and draw together.
And it dies.
No glow on their plate. No ring. The Warden sets his rod on one stand, then the other.
"Nothing, Penhale. Nothing, Penhale."
"Ghost!" the gallery roars, delighted, because for once it isn't us.
Dov stares at his own hands as if they've let him down. "That," he tells the Warden, "was a good Lamplighter."
"It was," says Sef. "They guessed right. Once. Watch the next."

The next two, the Panes go to the same chalked stands, because that's what the string told them, and the notes come through on gaps a hand wrong. They double both. Both brothers flinch like they've grabbed a pipe out of the furnace, and the Warden calls Marks off their stands, ring and Toll the hard way. After that they're holding enough to think twice. On Dov's fourth they body-block instead of drawing, and his Mordant shoves through the pair of them and Peals.
One to nothing.
Cullet throws cold, and it lands flat but inside the semitone. It goes through Marten's block, then mine, loses a weight on each of us and still rings three full counts. One all.
Dov answers with the Ferret, quick and mean, low along the wall. Two to one.
Then Cullet Raises again. Cold.
The voicing hits the stone and I have it. A three, by the shove of the bloom in front of it, and right on Oduya's peg. Not a hair off. That one Peals.
And mine is the only stand in the beam.
No pair. No time to make one. I could block it, and it would lose one weight going through me and ring anyway.
So I don't block it.
Palms out. Breath in.
It comes into me like a mallet onto a chisel head: the knock in the wrists, then the hum running up into the elbows and settling in my back teeth. My right ear, the good one, goes thin and high.
The Warden's rod touches my stand.
"Three held. Five, Halloway."
Five Marks. Forever. Three ring in my bones, for now.

I Ground it my way, heels then balls, one low hum straight down. A ring a Breath, and one more on each of Dov's throws. It's gone inside two Breaths. My hands come back. My teeth stop. Behind me Marten hums his lullaby to nobody. He has nothing to Ground. He hasn't drawn all night.
Frost throws one more cold before the Half and gets lucky with it. Sharp, but inside the semitone. Two all.
The Long Ground.
Both sides, feet planted, humming down into the stands. The Penhale brothers sound like a pair of split bellows. I've nothing left to Ground, so I stand in it anyway, because everyone does.
My hands are fine. My teeth are fine.
My right ear isn't.

It's not loud. It's a thread. A high thin whine like wind through a cracked sash, sitting on top of everything. The Warden walks the floor with his rod and reads my stand. "Nothing held, Halloway." I hear him through it, like through a wall.
Held ring clears at the Long Ground. Everyone knows that. It's in the rules. So whatever this is, it isn't held ring.
Sef comes over with his notebook open and doesn't look at it.
I turn my left side to him. Habit. Nothing goes in that side, so nothing comes out of it either.

"Sums," he says. "Four things. No. Three. One, Marten's thirty-seven on the Book. Three off Rung Out. Two, one hard note doubled is two Marks, and two of those finish him for life. Three, we've still got the Hounds to come, and the Hounds throw nothing but hard."
Marten looks at the floor for a long moment. "Aye, well."
He sits down on the bench by the stair as if he'd been waiting to be asked.
"So who stands with Wren?" says Dov, and then he hears himself, and goes a colour I've only seen on old mortar.
Sef doesn't answer. He just looks at him.
"No," says Dov. "I'm the Caller. I'm the Caller, that's what I am. Jory's fifteen. Jory's got soot up to the elbows. Jory's never..."
Jory, at the foot of the stair, is already taking off her coat.
"Callers live on the count," says Sef. "You Raise on a count, you voice on the next. You've got the best clock in this Drum, Dov. I just need it pointing the other way."
Dov opens his mouth to say something enormous. Nothing comes out. He walks very fast to the kiln ash bucket at the foot of the stair.
Which is where you came in.
"Kilnyard. Your registration for the second Half."
"Halloway and Carrick, Dampers. Tewkes on to Call."
Dov wipes his mouth on his sleeve. He walks onto his stand like it's a plank over a drop. Then he plants both feet and looks at me.
"What do I say?" he says. "When I count. What do you say?"
"Doesn't matter what. Matters that it's the same every time."
He thinks about it. Swallows.
"Three. Two. Carrick."
Of course it is.
Glasshouse throw first in the second Half, and the Gaffer has watched the bucket.

I see it in him. He's looking at Dov's face, grey as a hearthstone, and at Marten on the bench, and he has done his own sum. The good pair's broken. Kilnyard have a sick Caller where a Damper should be. Stop throwing cold. Start throwing true.
Frost Raises. And this time she hums.

It comes up through my soles like a hand round my ankle. High. A wave of two and a half paces, near enough, coming down our right side. I know the pair before I've finished knowing the note: the stand I'm on, and the one a pace and a quarter behind me along her path.
"Back one, Dov. Straight behind me."
He moves. The Raise ends. He's there.
I open my mouth to count.
I shut it.

The front comes on, glowing faintly in the bloom, walking pace, the way they always come. And everything in me wants to turn my head. Look at him. Check his palms are up. Check his breath. Hold back a hair and watch him start first.
That's what I did at Ropewalk. A hair. And Marten took a four alone.
I keep my eyes on the front. I keep my palms out.
"Three," says Dov, through the whine in my good ear. Loud. Louder than anything he's ever thrown. "Two. Carrick."
I draw on Carrick.
Nothing.
No mallet. No knock in the wrists. The note is there, and then there's a hole in the air the shape of a note, and a quiet so complete I can feel the bloom settle.
The Warden's rod. My stand. His.
"Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Carrick."
Dov makes a sound I've never heard a person make. Half laugh, half bucket.
Under my bare feet the floor does something small, after. I don't wait to feel what. I look at Sef.
"Again," says Sef.
Jory throws the way Dov does when he thinks nobody's watching. Quick lead-in, no fuss, no name.

Her first two rattle. On her third the Panes guess a pair, and for once it's the right one, and the note dies between them. "Ghost!" Two ghost quells all night for Glasshouse, out of I don't know how many guesses, and a lot of ring in the Penhale brothers' arms for the rest.
Jory goes red to the ears. Dov, from his stand, calls, "Again. Same again. They won't get it twice."
They don't. Her fifth goes in clean, true on their peg, rings three full counts.
Three to two.
"That," Dov shouts across the Drum, "is the Sootlight. It's hers. Nobody else is allowed it."
Jory looks at him as if he's handed her a crown.

Frost goes back to cold after that, twice, and Oduya keeps sliding the pot off the heat, and both rattle. Cullet throws a light one, wide, and Dov and I body-block it down to nothing. Then the Gaffer needs a Peal again, and he can only aim one true, so it's lead-ins.
Second Dead Air. "Three. Two. Carrick." Nothing.
I don't look at him. I don't look at him so hard my neck aches.
Last throw. Three to two. One Peal levels it for Glasshouse and sends us to Sudden Peal.

Cullet Raises with a lead-in, from the near wing, straight at the middle, where our Last Stand sits empty and rocking. The note comes up through the stone lower than I'd like. A wave of four and a half paces. Close to the bottom of what any pair can kill.

There's one pair for it. The two stands either side of the middle, and from Cullet's stand their difference along his path is two and a quarter paces. I've walked that pair a dozen times this week with a string of my own. The walls haven't moved. The pace hasn't moved. It's inside a tenth.
"Across, Dov. Your side of the middle."
He goes. He doesn't ask. The Raise closes.

The front is big. Slow and fat and lit like a lamp turned up. Hard, by the shove of the bloom. A four. If either of us draws first, whoever it is takes four ring and two Marks alone, and if it's Dov, those are the first Marks of his life.
"Three," says Dov. His voice cracks on it. "Two."
My hands want to go. All of me wants to go first, because first is safe, first is mine.
"Carrick."
We draw.
Silence. The real kind. The whole Drum, gallery and all, holding one breath.
"Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Carrick."
Then the noise comes down off the gallery, and I only get half of it, and it's still the loudest thing I've ever stood under.
Three to two, Kilnyard.

After. Gallery empty. Glasshouse gone up the stair with their string and their aching arms. Sef pays out the gate on the bench: one crown for me. Six of thirty-eight. I put it in my pocket and keep my hand on it.
Dov is sitting on his stand. Not standing on it. Sitting, cross-legged, the way you'd sit on a hearth.
"I didn't take a Mark," he says. To the floor, mostly.
"You didn't take a Mark."
"I want that written down somewhere."
Sef, who is holding his notebook, says "Done," and doesn't write anything.
"You counted it right," I say. "All three."
Dov looks up at me. He's waiting for the joke. I haven't got one.
"I drew on your count," I say. "I've never done that."
He nods, slowly. He doesn't name anything. That's how I know it landed.
Footsteps on the stair. Slow ones. A pause at the turn, where the gallery doesn't reach. Where an old man stood with his boots off in Round 1, his palm flat on the wall.
Then the footsteps keep coming.
Bartholomew Quist steps off the bottom stair and onto the floor of the Kilnyard Drum.
Thirty-one years since his bad night, he told us. I'd bet my tin he hasn't set foot on a Drum floor since.
Sef goes very still. Marten stands up off the bench. Nobody says anything. He wouldn't hear it, and he isn't watching our mouths. He's watching the floor.

He sits on the bottom step. Unlaces his boots. Sets them side by side, neatly, the way they sat beside him on that stair the first night. Then he walks across the Drum barefoot, slow, like a man crossing ice, and steps up onto the Last Stand.
It rocks under him. A finger's breadth. I hear it knock flat.
He doesn't step off. He plants both feet the way I plant mine, heels then balls, and puts his weight down, and stands there with his eyes shut, like a man listening for something a long way off.
Then he opens them. He looks at me. Not at Dov. Not at Sef.
"Again," he says. "Show me again."
